title: The present subjunctive
objectives: I can explain what the subjunctive mood is, why Portuguese needs it, and how a que clause differs from an infinitive.
I can form the present subjunctive of regular, irregular and spelling-change verbs, and say why each form is spelled as it is.
I can express wishes, requests, hopes and emotions with querer que, esperar que, pedir que, lamentar que and tomara que.
I can choose between an infinitive (same subject) and que + subjunctive (different subject).
I can use talvez with the subjunctive and common blessings and fixed expressions such as Que Deus te abençoe and Bom proveito.

vocabulary.note: English says 'I want you to come', with an object and an infinitive. Portuguese has no such pattern: after querer you build a whole clause introduced by que (that), with its own verb, so the word for word version is 'I want that you come'. Quero is said KE-ru: qu before e is the sound k with a silent u, and the final o is said u. The à in the example is the preposition a (to) fused with the article a (the).

example.pt: Quero que você venha à minha festa.
example.en: I want you to come to my party.
example.literal: I-want that you come to-the my party.

vocabulary.en: to hope that, to expect that
vocabulary.note: One verb covers three English verbs: esperar is to wait for, to hope and to expect, and the sentence decides which. Followed by que and a new subject it means to hope or to expect. The pronunciation of the first e is often said like i in speech (is-pe-RAR).

example.pt: Espero que ela goste do presente.
example.en: I hope she likes the gift.
example.literal: I-hope that she like of-the gift.

vocabulary.note: Pedir is to ask for something or to request an action; to ask a question is perguntar. Its eu form is irregular: peço, with the d of the stem replaced by ç (the s sound before o). The present subjunctive peça is built from peço, so it keeps the ç.

example.pt: Peço que você fale mais devagar.
example.en: I ask you to speak more slowly.
example.literal: I-request that you speak more slow.

vocabulary.note: Said de-ze-ZHAR: a single s between vowels is z, and j is the zh sound of English 'measure'. Desejar is used for wishes about other people, so it is a natural trigger for the subjunctive.

example.pt: Desejo que você seja muito feliz.
example.en: I wish for you to be very happy.
example.literal: I-wish that you be very happy.

vocabulary.en: I hope that, let's hope that
vocabulary.note: Tomara is a frozen exclamation traditionally linked to the verb tomar (to take); speakers no longer hear the verb in it, so there is no useful word for word gloss. It works like English 'if only' or 'would that'. Alone, Tomara! means 'Let's hope so!'. It is said to-MA-ra, stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the default for a word ending in a. Chova is the subjunctive of chover (to rain), and sábado is stressed on the third to last syllable, which is why it has an accent.

example.pt: Tomara que não chova no sábado.
example.en: I hope it doesn't rain on Saturday.
example.literal: Tomara that not rain on-the Saturday.

vocabulary.note: One word made from tal (such) and vez (time, occasion): 'at such a time it may be'. It is said taw-VEZ, because an l that closes a syllable is said w, and it is stressed on the last syllable (the default for a word ending in z), so it has no accent. Placed before its verb, talvez takes the subjunctive.

example.pt: Talvez ele chegue atrasado.
example.en: Maybe he will arrive late.
example.literal: Such-time he arrive late.

vocabulary.en: to root for, to hope that
vocabulary.note: Torcer literally means to twist or wring. The usual explanation is that early football fans twisted their handkerchiefs with nerves; that is why it means to cheer for a team or hope for someone's success. In speech: Tô torcendo por você! (I'm rooting for you!), where tô is a spoken shortening of estou. The ç of torço is the s sound before o. Consigam comes from conseguir (to manage, to succeed): see the spelling note on consonant changes.

example.pt: Torço para que vocês consigam a vaga.
example.en: I'm rooting for you to get the position.
example.literal: I-twist for that you-all manage the vacancy.

vocabulary.note: Dar is to give and certo is right or correct. The thing that works out is the subject: Tudo deu certo (everything gave right) means everything worked out. Dar is irregular in the subjunctive: dê, with an accent explained in the irregular verbs note.

example.pt: Espero que tudo dê certo.
example.en: I hope everything works out.
example.literal: I-hope that everything give right.

vocabulary.en: to be sorry about, to regret
vocabulary.note: Lamentar expresses sorrow about something bad; it is not the apology 'sorry', which is desculpa. In doente the en before a consonant is a nasal vowel, and the t before the final e (said i) becomes tch: do-EN-tchi.

example.pt: Lamento que você esteja doente.
example.en: I'm sorry you are ill.
example.literal: I-lament that you be sick.

vocabulary.note: Saudade has no exact English equivalent: it is the ache of missing a person, a place or a time. You can say sentir saudade de or ter saudade de (to have longing of). Said sau-DA-de: au is a diphthong, so there are three syllables, the stress is on the second to last as the ending e predicts, and the final e sounds like i. Família is stressed on the third to last syllable (fa-MÍ-lia), so it has an accent.

example.pt: Sinto saudade da minha família.
example.en: I miss my family.
example.literal: I-feel longing of-the my family.

vocabulary.note: From esperar. Said es-pe-RAN-ça: the an before a consonant is a nasal vowel, and ç is the s sound before a. Note the pattern ter esperança de que (to have hope that), which is followed by the subjunctive like the verb.

example.pt: Ainda tenho esperança de que ele volte.
example.en: I still have hope that he will come back.
example.literal: Still I-have hope of that he return.

vocabulary.note: From desejar, said de-ZE-zhu. After é que a wish is still a wish, so the subjunctive follows.

example.pt: Meu maior desejo é que minha família esteja bem.
example.en: My greatest wish is for my family to be well.
example.literal: My biggest wish is that my family be well.

vocabulary.note: From pedir. Said pe-JI-du: the d before an i is said like the j of 'jeans'. In a restaurant, um pedido is also an order. Não ... nada is a double negative, which is normal in Portuguese.

example.pt: Ele fez um pedido: que a gente não conte nada.
example.en: He made one request: that we not say anything.
example.literal: He made a request: that the-people not tell nothing.

vocabulary.note: Ficar means to stay, and before an adjective it means to become or to feel: ficar feliz is to become happy, to be glad. The eu form is fico and the subjunctive is fique (see the spelling note on consonant changes).

example.pt: Fico feliz que você goste da casa.
example.en: I'm glad you like the house.
example.literal: I-stay happy that you like of-the house.

vocabulary.note: Ter medo is to have fear, where English uses to be afraid. The careful form is ter medo de que; in speech people often drop de. Se machucar is reflexive (to hurt oneself, to get hurt), and its subjunctive machuque has qu to keep the k sound before e.

example.pt: Tenho medo que ele se machuque.
example.en: I'm afraid he will get hurt.
example.literal: I-have fear that he himself hurt.

vocabulary.note: Said a-ben-ço-AR: ben is a nasal syllable (en before a consonant), and ç is the s sound before o. In the subjunctive abençoe, o and e are both strong vowels, so they are two syllables, a-ben-ÇO-e, not a diphthong.

example.pt: Que Deus abençoe sua família.
example.en: May God bless your family.
example.literal: That God bless your family.

vocabulary.en: to enjoy, to make the most of
vocabulary.note: Built on proveito (benefit, advantage). Aproveite is both the command for você and the present subjunctive, because the imperative borrows the subjunctive forms. In aproveitar, ei is a diphthong: a-pro-vei-TAR.

example.pt: Aproveite a viagem!
example.en: Enjoy the trip!
example.literal: Take-advantage-of the trip!

vocabulary.note: Ter cuidado is also used. Tome is from tomar (tomo, tome). In cuidado the ui is a diphthong: cui-DA-do.

example.pt: Peço que você tome cuidado na estrada.
example.en: I ask you to be careful on the road.
example.literal: I-request that you take care on-the road.

vocabulary.note: Confiar always takes em before the person: confiar em alguém. Precisar que (to need that) is one more trigger for the subjunctive. Mim ends in an im, which is a nasal i: the lips do not close at the end.

example.pt: Preciso que você confie em mim.
example.en: I need you to trust me.
example.literal: I-need that you trust in me.

vocabulary.note: Permitir que is a trigger because allowing is about an act that has not happened yet. Ninguém (nobody) stays alongside não before the verb: a double negative is standard in Portuguese. Comigo is the one word for 'with me'.

example.pt: Não permito que ninguém fale assim comigo.
example.en: I don't allow anyone to talk to me like that.
example.literal: Not I-permit that nobody speak thus with-me.

vocabulary.note: Said SOR-tchi: the t before the final e, which sounds like i, becomes tch.

example.pt: Boa sorte na entrevista!
example.en: Good luck in the interview!

vocabulary.note: Bom proveito! is said to someone who is about to eat or is enjoying something. Said pro-VEI-tu: ei is a diphthong and the final o is said u.

example.pt: Bom proveito!
example.en: Enjoy your meal!
example.literal: Good benefit!

dialogues.title: Antes da viagem
dialogues.context: Pedro is about to travel to Salvador for work. His mother, Lúcia, helps him pack and worries a little.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Pedro, você já arrumou a mala? Quero que você leve um casaco.
lines.en: Pedro, have you packed your suitcase yet? I want you to take a coat.
lines.literal: Pedro, you already arranged the suitcase? I-want that you take a coat.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Mãe, vai fazer calor em Salvador. Eu não preciso de casaco.
lines.en: Mom, it's going to be hot in Salvador. I don't need a coat.
lines.literal: Mother, it-goes to-make heat in Salvador. I not need of coat.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Talvez faça frio à noite. Peço que você leve, por favor.
lines.en: Maybe it will be cold at night. I ask you to take it, please.
lines.literal: Such-time it-make cold at-the night. I-request that you take, for favor.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Tá bom, eu levo. Mas espero que você não fique preocupada o tempo todo.
lines.en: Okay, I'll take it. But I hope you won't be worried the whole time.
lines.literal: Is good, I take. But I-hope that you not stay worried the time all.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Eu só quero que você tome cuidado. E quero que você me ligue todos os dias.
lines.en: I just want you to be careful. And I want you to call me every day.
lines.literal: I only want that you take care. And I-want that you me call all the days.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Pode deixar. Tomara que o voo não atrase.
lines.en: Don't worry. I hope the flight isn't delayed.
lines.literal: Can leave. Tomara that the flight not delay.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Que Deus te abençoe, meu filho. Vai com Deus.
lines.en: May God bless you, my son. Go with God.
lines.literal: That God you bless, my son. Go with God.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Obrigado, mãe. Já estou com saudade.
lines.en: Thanks, Mom. I already miss you.
lines.literal: Obliged, mother. Already I-am with longing.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Eu também. Boa viagem, meu filho!
lines.en: Me too. Have a good trip, my son!

dialogues.title: Jantar com surpresas
dialogues.context: Rodrigo takes his friend Camila to a new restaurant. The waiter, Marcos, serves them.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.pt: Camila, eu quero que você conheça este restaurante. Espero que goste.
lines.en: Camila, I want you to get to know this restaurant. I hope you like it.
lines.literal: Camila, I want that you know this restaurant. I-hope that like.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Já estou com fome! Tomara que a comida seja tão boa quanto dizem.
lines.en: I'm already hungry! I hope the food is as good as they say.
lines.literal: Already I-am with hunger! Tomara that the food be so good as they-say.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Boa noite! Querem que eu traga o cardápio agora?
lines.en: Good evening! Would you like me to bring the menu now?
lines.literal: Good night! You-all-want that I bring the menu now?

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.pt: Sim, por favor. E peço que traga também uma água sem gás.
lines.en: Yes, please. And I ask you to bring a still water as well.
lines.literal: Yes, for favor. And I-request that bring also a water without gas.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Talvez eu peça o peixe. Você recomenda?
lines.en: Maybe I'll order the fish. Do you recommend it?
lines.literal: Such-time I ask-for the fish. You recommend?

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Recomendo, sim. Mas talvez demore uns vinte minutos.
lines.en: I do, yes. But it may take about twenty minutes.
lines.literal: I-recommend, yes. But such-time take some twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.pt: Sem problema. Queremos aproveitar a noite.
lines.en: No problem. We want to enjoy the evening.
lines.literal: Without problem. We-want to-take-advantage-of the night.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Aqui estão os pratos de vocês. Bom proveito!
lines.en: Here are your dishes. Enjoy your meal!
lines.literal: Here are the dishes of you-all. Good benefit!

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Obrigada! Hum, que delícia. Rodrigo, fico feliz que a gente esteja aqui.
lines.en: Thank you! Mmm, how delicious. Rodrigo, I'm glad we're here.
lines.literal: Obliged! Hm, what delight. Rodrigo, I-stay happy that the-people be here.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.pt: Que bom! Quero que a gente volte aqui no mês que vem.
lines.en: Great! I want us to come back here next month.
lines.literal: What good! I-want that the-people return here in-the month that comes.

dialogues.title: A véspera da entrevista
dialogues.context: Fernanda has a job interview tomorrow. Her friend Lívia and her brother Tiago try to calm her down.

lines.speaker: Lívia
lines.pt: Amanhã é a entrevista, né? Espero que dê tudo certo.
lines.en: The interview is tomorrow, right? I hope everything goes well.
lines.literal: Tomorrow is the interview, no-is? I-hope that give everything right.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Estou nervosa. Tenho medo que a entrevistadora não goste de mim.
lines.en: I'm nervous. I'm afraid the interviewer won't like me.
lines.literal: I-am nervous. I-have fear that the interviewer not like of me.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.pt: Calma, Fê. Você é muito preparada. Quero que você durma cedo hoje.
lines.en: Calm down, Fê. You're very well prepared. I want you to sleep early today.
lines.literal: Calm, Fê. You are very prepared. I-want that you sleep early today.

lines.speaker: Lívia
lines.pt: Isso mesmo. Talvez você fique ansiosa, mas respira fundo e confia em você.
lines.en: Exactly. Maybe you'll feel anxious, but breathe deeply and trust yourself.
lines.literal: That same. Such-time you stay anxious, but breathe deep and trust in you.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Tomara que eu consiga ficar calma. Peço que vocês não contem pra ninguém, tá?
lines.en: I hope I can stay calm. I ask you not to tell anyone, okay?
lines.literal: Tomara that I manage to-stay calm. I-request that you-all not tell to nobody, is?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.pt: Pode deixar, é segredo nosso. Torço para que você consiga a vaga.
lines.en: Don't worry, it's our secret. I'm rooting for you to get the position.
lines.literal: Can leave, is secret ours. I-twist for that you manage the vacancy.

lines.speaker: Lívia
lines.pt: Boa sorte, amiga! Me liga depois, tá? Quero que você me conte tudo.
lines.en: Good luck, my friend! Call me afterwards, okay? I want you to tell me everything.
lines.literal: Good luck, friend! Me call afterwards, is? I-want that you me tell everything.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Ligo, sim. Obrigada por tudo. Que bom que vocês existem!
lines.en: I will. Thanks for everything. How great that you two exist!
lines.literal: I-call, yes. Obliged for everything. What good that you-all exist!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This unit adds no new spelling rule. Every accent mark, nasal vowel and unusual letter in its words follows a rule from the first three lessons, and this note applies those rules to the new words so that you can read and write them instead of memorizing them. Two questions solve almost every word. First, where is the stress, and does it agree with the default for the word's ending? Words ending in a, e or o (with or without s) and in am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and most other endings are stressed on the last syllable; a written accent appears on the stressed vowel when the stress disagrees with the default. Second, what do the neighboring letters say about how a letter is pronounced? The letters c and g, the pairs qu and gu, a vowel followed by m or n, and the digraphs nh, lh and ch are all decided by what surrounds them.

Accents on short words. A stressed word of one syllable that ends in a, e or o (with or without s) always takes an accent: vá (go, from ir), dê (give, from dar), já (already), gás (gas), mês (month), Fê (a nickname for Fernanda), nós (we), só (only), né (short for não é, 'isn't it'), tá (short for está, 'okay') and tô (short for estou, 'I am'). The mark is chosen by the sound. Dê, Fê, mês and tô have a closed vowel (the e of English 'say', the o of 'go'), so they take the circumflex; né, só and nós have the open e of 'bed' or the open o of 'law', and tá and já have the open a of 'father', so they take the acute. The accent on dê also separates it from de, the unstressed little word that means 'of' and is said like 'jee'.

Accents on long words. Stress on the third to last syllable always needs an accent, because no ending predicts it: Lúcia and Lívia (LÚ-ci-a, LÍ-vi-a), cardápio (car-DÁ-pi-o), delícia (de-LÍ-ci-a), véspera (VÉS-pe-ra), trânsito (TRÂN-si-to), último (ÚL-ti-mo), sábado (SÁ-ba-do), ônibus (Ô-ni-bus), simpáticos (sim-PÁ-ti-cos) and Florianópolis (Flo-ri-a-NÓ-po-lis). A word that ends in a glide plus a vowel counts the i or u as a syllable of its own, so água (Á-gu-a) and família (fa-MÍ-li-a) are written with an accent for the same reason. The circumflex in trânsito marks the closed a that appears before m or n. In the opposite direction, ninguém (nin-GUÉM) and difíceis (di-FÍ-ceis) are stressed away from the default of their endings (em defaults to the second to last syllable, is to the last), so each needs a mark. In ninguém the mark shows only the stress; the nasal sound comes from the m, and the u after g is silent because gu before e is the hard g.

Vowels side by side. Two strong vowels (a, e, o) never make a diphthong, so each keeps its own beat: voo is VO-o, deem (they give) is DE-em, abençoe is a-ben-ÇO-e and preocupada is pre-o-cu-PA-da. Older spelling wrote a circumflex on vôo and dêem; the 2009 reform removed it, because the stress falls where the default predicts. A diphthong is a weak i or u beside a strong vowel, said in a single syllable: Deus (DEUS), proveito (pro-VEI-to), cuidado (cui-DA-do), peixe (PEI-xe), queira (QUEI-ra), saiba (SAI-ba) and arrumou (ar-ru-MOU).

Nasal vowels. A tilde or an m or n that closes a syllable makes the vowel nasal. Mãe is one syllable, like English 'eye' said through the nose; amanhã is a-ma-NHÃ, where the tilde shows both the nasal sound and the stress, so nothing more is needed; and vão, like the verb ending -am of falam, is the nasal glide ão. At the end of a word, em is a nasal e with a y glide: bem, vem, sem, viagem, ninguém and the verb endings in existem. Im at the end of a word, as in mim, is a nasal i. Before a consonant, an, en, in, on and un are nasal vowels and the n is not pronounced as a consonant: esperança, doente, vinte, confiar, onde. Compare com (nasal, the lips do not close) with comigo (co-MI-go), where the m is followed by a vowel and is an ordinary m.

Consonants decided by neighbors. The sound of c and g depends on the next letter: hard before a, o, u, soft before e, i. Qu and gu before e or i keep the hard sound and the u is normally silent: que, quero, queira, aqui, ligue, pague. In a few words the u is pronounced (cinquenta, tranquilo), so those are learned as words. The cedilla gives the s sound before a, o or u: abençoe, torço, peço, esperança, faça, conheça. Gu before a is pronounced gw: água. J is always the zh of 'measure' (desejo, seja, esteja) and h on its own is always silent (haja, hoje). Nh and lh are single sounds: venha, tenha, filho, sonhou. X has several values, and the ones in this unit's words are these: after ei it is sh (peixe, deixar), in ex before a vowel it is z (existem, e-ZIS-tem), and before a consonant it is s (sexta). A single s between vowels is z (casaco, desejar), and ss between vowels is s (possa). An l that closes a syllable is said w: talvez (taw-VEZ), Natal (na-TAW), falta (FAW-ta). In most of Brazil a t or d before the sound i, which includes a final e said i, becomes tch or j (the j of 'jeans'): noite, vinte, Tiago, simpáticos, pedido, sorte.

Crase. The accent in à is the grave, which has one job: the preposition a (to) and the article a (the) fuse into à. In venha à minha festa and vá à praia, the words are 'to the my party' and 'to the beach'. The test: if you would say ao with a masculine noun (vou ao restaurante), the feminine noun takes à.

VÁ, DÊ, JÁ, GÁS, MÊS, FÊ, NÓS, SÓ, NÉ, TÁ, TÔ
A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o (with or without s) takes an accent. Circumflex for a closed e or o, acute for an open e or o and for a.
Lúcia, Lívia, cardápio, delícia, véspera, sábado, último, ônibus, simpáticos
Stress on the third to last syllable always takes an accent. The endings ia and io count as two syllables.
Glide plus vowel at the end counts as two syllables, so the stress is third from last. Gu before a is said gw.
Third to last stress. The circumflex marks the closed a before n, and the an is a nasal vowel.
Stress against the default of the ending. The u after g before e is silent.
Two strong vowels side by side are two syllables. The circumflex of vôo and dêem was dropped in 2009.
Deus, proveito, cuidado, peixe, deixar, queira, saiba, arrumou
A weak i or u beside a strong vowel is one syllable. X after ei is sh.
The tilde makes a vowel nasal and, with no other accent, marks the stress. The ending -am is a weak nasal glide.
bem, sem, vem, viagem, existem, mim, com
bẽj̃, sẽj̃, vẽj̃, vi-A-gẽj̃, mĩ, kõ
Em at the end of a word is a nasal e with a y glide; im is a nasal i; om is a nasal o. The final m closes no lips.
An, en, in, on, un before a consonant are nasal vowels; the n is not a separate consonant.
The cedilla gives the s sound before a, o, u, where c alone would be k. Before e and i the plain c already says s (certo, delícia).
que, quero, queira, aqui, ligue, pague
ke, KE-ru, KEI-ra, a-KI, LI-gi, PA-gi
Qu and gu before e or i keep the hard k and g; the u is silent.
J is always zh (the s of 'measure'); h is silent; a single s between vowels is z.
Nh is one sound like ny in canyon; lh is one sound like lli in million.
An l that closes a syllable is said w. Final z gives last syllable stress, so no accent is needed.
In most of Brazil, a t or d before the sound i (an i or a weak final e) becomes tch or j.
ss between vowels is s; a single s between vowels is z; ex before a vowel is z; x before a consonant is s; x after ei is sh.
Crase: the preposition a fused with the article a. The grave shows the fusion, not the stress.

examples.pt: Quero que a gente vá à praia no sábado.
examples.en: I want us to go to the beach on Saturday.
examples.literal: I-want that the-people go to-the beach on-the Saturday.

examples.pt: Espero que a água esteja gelada.
examples.en: I hope the water is cold.
examples.literal: I-hope that the water be iced.

examples.pt: Lamento que você não possa vir.
examples.en: I'm sorry you can't come.
examples.literal: I-lament that you not can come.

examples.pt: Tomara que o ônibus não atrase.
examples.en: I hope the bus isn't late.
examples.literal: Tomara that the bus not delay.

examples.pt: Peço que você deixe o peixe na geladeira.
examples.en: I ask you to leave the fish in the fridge.
examples.literal: I-request that you leave the fish in-the fridge.

grammar.title: The subjunctive mood: what it says and why Portuguese needs it
grammar.explanation:
A mood is the way a verb shows how the speaker regards an action: as a plain fact (the indicative, which every lesson so far has used), as a command (the imperative), or as something that is not stated as fact (the subjunctive). The principle behind the subjunctive is that the indicative asserts and the subjunctive does not assert. Sei que ela mora aqui (I know she lives here) reports a fact, so mora is indicative. Quero que ela more aqui (I want her to live here) does not say that she lives here; it says what the speaker wants, so more is subjunctive. Wish, request, hope, fear, permission, doubt and emotional reaction all have this in common: the event is wished for, asked for, worried about or judged, rather than reported.

To see where the mood sits you need one more grammar term. A clause is a group of words built around one verb and its subject. Quero que você venha has two clauses: the main clause Quero, which could stand alone, and the subordinate clause que você venha, which depends on the main clause for its meaning. The word que is a conjunction (a joining word) meaning 'that'. English can drop 'that' (I hope she comes); Portuguese never can (Espero que ela venha). The subjunctive verb stands in the subordinate clause, and the meaning of the main clause decides whether it is needed. A word or expression in the main clause that calls for the subjunctive is called a trigger: querer que, esperar que, pedir que, tomara que and the others in this unit.

English does the same job in other ways, which is why the subjunctive feels unfamiliar. After 'want' English uses an object and an infinitive (I want you to come), after 'hope' an ordinary present (I hope she comes), and for blessings the helper 'may' (May God bless you). A few true subjunctive forms survive: 'I suggest that he be on time' and 'If I were you' use be and were instead of is and was, and 'God save the Queen' uses save instead of saves. Portuguese kept the mood alive in every verb and every person, so its forms are a working part of everyday speech. In particular Portuguese has no 'I want you to come' pattern: after querer you must build a whole clause, Quero que você venha.

Two points about the name. The present subjunctive is the present-tense set of forms of the subjunctive mood, built from the present indicative; the name does not mean the event is happening now. Espero que ele chegue amanhã talks about tomorrow and chegue is present subjunctive. Time is read from the context, and from the main verb's point of view the event is usually now or later. The subjunctive also has an imperfect and a future, which later units teach; this unit needs only the present.

You already know these forms. The imperative for você and vocês (Fale! Não faça isso!) is built from the present subjunctive, as the imperative lesson showed. What is new here is using the same forms inside a que clause after a trigger.

grammar.title: Forming the present subjunctive: the opposite vowel
grammar.explanation:
The present subjunctive is built from the present indicative by one procedure. Take the eu form of the present (falo, como, parto), remove the final -o to leave the stem, then add the subjunctive ending. The ending vowel is the opposite of the indicative one: -ar verbs take e, and -er and -ir verbs take a. In the indicative, falar has a (fala, falamos) and comer has e (come, comemos); in the subjunctive they trade places (fale, falemos; coma, comamos). The swap is the signal. Fala and fale differ by one vowel, and so do come and coma, so train your ear on the final vowel: it alone tells you that the speaker is not stating a fact.

The endings are therefore -e, -e, -emos, -em for -ar verbs and -a, -a, -amos, -am for -er and -ir verbs, for the persons eu, você (ele, ela, a gente), nós and vocês (eles, elas). The eu and você forms are identical, which is why the pronoun is normally spoken in a que clause when the subject could be unclear. In the regions that use tu, the tu form ends in -es or -as (fales, comas, partas). A gente takes the você form: Quero que a gente fale.

Why start from the eu form? Because it is the one present form that carries the verb's irregularities: faço, digo, tenho, venho, ponho, saio, ouço, peço, posso, vejo, trago, conheço, durmo. In the subjunctive every person is built on that one stem, so the irregularity appears everywhere: faça, faças, faça, façamos, façam. In the present indicative only some persons show it (fazemos, dormimos, pedimos keep the infinitive stem), so the subjunctive is in this respect more regular than the indicative: one stem, one set of endings. Faça, diga, tenha, venha, ponha, saia, ouça, peça, possa, veja, traga, conheça and durma all follow at once.

Stress. Every regular subjunctive form is stressed on the second to last syllable (fa-LE-mos, co-MA-mos), which is the default for endings in e, a, os and em/am, so none of them carries a written accent. This contrasts with the imperfect of the A2 lessons (falávamos), whose stress falls third from last and so needs an accent. The only accents in present subjunctive forms belong to two one-syllable irregulars, vá and dê, in the next notes.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: consonant changes in subjunctive forms
grammar.explanation:
A spelling change in a subjunctive form is not an exception to the procedure; it is the spelling rules of the first lesson doing their work. Those rules say that c and g are hard (k, g) before a, o, u and soft (s, zh) before e, i. In an -ar verb the ending changes from a or o to e, so a stem ending in c or g would change its sound unless the letters are adjusted. Portuguese keeps the sound of the stem and changes the letters, using tools you already have: qu, gu and the cedilla.

Three cases in -ar verbs. Verbs in -car change c to qu: ficar, fico, fique. Without the change the form would be fice, read fi-si. Verbs in -gar change g to gu: pagar, pago, pague. Without it the form would be page, read pa-zhi. Verbs in -çar lose the cedilla: começar, começo, comece. The cedilla exists only to make the s sound before a, o, u, and before e the plain c already says s. The same reasoning turns machucar into machuque and ligar into ligue. The sound of the stem is the same in every person; only the letters change.

The opposite situation in -er and -ir verbs. There the ending changes from o to a, and both are hard-side vowels, so no new change is needed. But many of these verbs already changed their spelling in the eu form, because the infinitive has a soft vowel: conhecer has a soft c, so the eu form needs a cedilla to keep it (conheço), and the subjunctive conheça keeps it. Proteger has a soft g, written j before o or a (protejo, proteja). Dirigir becomes dirijo and dirija. The reverse happens in seguir: the u of gu is needed only before e or i, so it disappears before o and a (sigo, siga), and the same is true of conseguir (consigo, consiga). Esquecer gives esqueço and esqueça. In each case the eu-form stem decides, and the subjunctive simply follows it.

A third kind of change is a change of stem vowel or consonant inside the verb itself. Dormir has durmo in the eu form and so durma throughout: durma, durmamos, durmam. Pedir has peço and peça, peçamos. Sentir has sinto and sinta, sintamos; vestir has visto and vista; ouvir has ouço and ouça; poder has posso and possa. The nós form follows the eu stem too (peçamos, not pedamos), which is where the subjunctive differs from the present indicative (pedimos, sentimos, dormimos).

grammar.title: Irregular verbs in the present subjunctive
grammar.explanation:
The eu-form procedure works for nearly every verb, including the ones with an irregular present (fazer, dizer, ter, vir, pôr, sair, ver, trazer, ouvir), because their eu form still ends in -o and gives a stem. It fails for seven verbs. For six of them, the eu form does not end in a plain -o that can be dropped: sou, estou, vou, dou, sei, hei. For querer, whose eu form quero would predict quera, the subjunctive queira is simply irregular. These seven have to be memorized: ser (seja), estar (esteja), ir (vá), dar (dê), saber (saiba), querer (queira) and haver (haja).

Some patterns help. Ser, estar and haver all end in -ja (seja, esteja, haja), and the other persons use the same stem: sejamos, estejamos, hajamos, sejam, estejam, hajam. Saber becomes saiba and querer becomes queira, again with the stem shared by all persons: saibamos, queiramos. Ir and dar have very short forms. The one-syllable vá and dê carry an accent because they are stressed one-syllable words ending in a vowel (see the spelling note); the circumflex on dê shows the closed e and keeps it apart from de, 'of'. The nós and vocês forms are vamos and vão for ir, demos and deem for dar. Deem has no accent: the circumflex of the old dêem was dropped in 2009, and the stress on the first e is where the ending em predicts it.

A trap: the nós form of ir, vamos, is identical to the present indicative, so Talvez nós vamos ao cinema is subjunctive even though it looks like the present. In speech a gente plus the singular is usual anyway (Talvez a gente vá). Haja is the subjunctive of the existential há, 'there is', so Tomara que haja lugar means 'I hope there is room'; in everyday speech people use ter instead (Tomara que tenha lugar).

English shows its subjunctive only faintly: with most verbs only in the third person singular (that he go, not goes), and fully with to be (that he be, if I were). To be is the verb behind seja and esteja, which are by far the most frequent irregular subjunctives, because nearly every expression of hope, doubt or emotion contains ser or estar. The old distinction between the two stays alive: Espero que ela seja feliz is about her life in general, and Espero que ela esteja feliz is about how she feels now.

grammar.title: Triggers, same subject and different subject
grammar.explanation:
The subjunctive is called for by the meaning of the main clause, not by the word que. Que also follows verbs of knowing, saying and seeing, and those take the indicative. The test is whether the main clause reports the content of the que clause as a fact. If it does (Sei que, Vejo que, Ele diz que), use the indicative: Sei que ela mora aqui. If the main clause wants, asks, hopes, fears, allows, or reacts to the content, use the subjunctive: Espero que ela more aqui.

The triggers fall into families. Will and preference: querer que, desejar que, preferir que, precisar que. Request and permission: pedir que, permitir que. Hope and fear: esperar que, torcer para que, tomara que, ter medo (de) que. Emotion: lamentar que, ficar feliz que. Possibility: talvez, placed before its verb, which is its normal position; the event is possible but not asserted. The emotion triggers may look odd, because the speaker is often sure the thing is true: in Fico feliz que você goste da cidade, you do like it. The mood marks that the speaker is reacting to the fact, not reporting it.

The second condition is a change of subject. When the same person wants and acts, the infinitive is enough, because there is no second person to name: Quero viajar. When the subject changes, the second verb needs its own subject and its own ending, so Portuguese builds a que clause: Quero que você viaje. English hides this difference, since it says 'I want to travel' and 'I want you to travel' with the same to-infinitive; Portuguese shows it. The same split applies to esperar (Espero chegar cedo, Espero que ele chegue cedo), to lamentar (Lamento não poder ir, Lamento que você não possa ir) and to ter medo (Tenho medo de errar, Tenho medo que ela erre).

With pedir, a spoken alternative is common in Brazil: Pedi pra ele ficar, with the infinitive. The formal version, Pedi que ele ficasse, uses a form of the subjunctive taught in a later unit, so for now use the present: Peço que ele fique.

grammar.title: Blessings and fixed expressions
grammar.explanation:
A blessing or a wish is a que clause standing alone, with the main verb left out: Que Deus te abençoe is Eu desejo que Deus te abençoe with the opening removed. The que that remains is the same conjunction as before, and the subjunctive stays because the clause is still a wish. English reaches the same meaning with the helper 'may' (May God bless you); Portuguese needs no helper, only que and the subjunctive. So Que você seja feliz is 'May you be happy', and Que tudo dê certo is 'May everything work out'. Negative wishes keep não before the verb: Que não chova. Blessings with Deus are extremely common in Brazil, even in casual speech.

Careful: the same letters que appear in a second, unrelated construction. In Que bom!, Que pena! and Que delícia!, que is an exclamation word meaning 'what' or 'how', followed by an adjective or noun and no verb at all. Que bom que você veio! has both: the first que is the exclamation 'how', the second is the conjunction 'that'. After such reactions the choice of mood is looser than after fico feliz que. For an event that is over and known, as in Que bom que você veio and Que bom que vocês existem, speakers normally use the indicative. For something present or possible, the subjunctive is also heard: Que pena que você não possa vir.

Other formulas belong to the same social situations but contain no verb: Boa viagem! (Have a good trip!), Boa sorte! (Good luck!), Bom proveito! (Enjoy your meal!) and Parabéns! (Congratulations!, said pa-ra-BÉNS, with an accent because the stress falls on the last syllable although ens defaults to the second to last). Saúde! (said after a sneeze, sa-Ú-de) also has no verb. Only the first group changes with the person: Que Deus abençoe vocês, Que Deus te acompanhe.

Tomara! alone is a complete answer meaning 'Let's hope so!'. Add que when you say what you hope for: Tomara que dê certo. Tomara que always requires the subjunctive.

culture.title: Blessings, saudade and wishing people well
culture.text:
Wishes and blessings are woven into Brazilian daily life. People say Deus te abençoe when thanking someone, Vai com Deus when a person leaves, and Se Deus quiser when talking about plans. These expressions are cultural and often religious, but many people use them as warm, everyday formulas, not only the devout. A mother may say Deus te abençoe to her adult child after any phone call.

Translation and usage come apart in these phrases, so it helps to keep them separate. Deus te abençoe is word for word 'God you bless' and in use it is a warm thank you or goodbye. Vai com Deus is word for word 'Go with God' and is said to anyone leaving, believer or not. Se Deus quiser is word for word 'If God wants' and is used like 'God willing' or simply 'hopefully' about plans; quiser is a form of the future subjunctive, which a later unit teaches, so for now learn the phrase as a unit.

Brazilians also wish each other good things with short set phrases: Bom proveito! to someone about to eat, Boa viagem! to a traveler, Boa sorte! before an exam, and Saúde! after a sneeze. The verb torcer is special: it literally means to twist, but Tô torcendo por você! means 'I'm rooting for you' and is used for football, exams, interviews and romances alike.

The word saudade deserves its own mention. It is the ache of missing a person, a place or a time, and it appears constantly in music, letters and goodbyes: Vou sentir saudade. Combined with the present subjunctive, it makes emotional, polite requests such as Quero que você me ligue or Espero que a gente se veja logo.

exercises.explanation: Estar (estou) is irregular: esteja. Lamentar is an emotion trigger.

exercises.prompt: Talvez ele ___ hoje.
exercises.explanation: Talvez before the verb takes the subjunctive: venho gives venha.

exercises.hint_en: Maybe we will go to the cinema today. Verb: ir.
exercises.explanation: The nós form of ir in the subjunctive is vamos, identical to the indicative.

exercises.prompt_en: I want you to call me.

exercises.prompt: What do you say to someone who is about to eat?
exercises.explanation: Bom proveito! literally wishes 'good benefit', and in use it wishes someone an enjoyable meal.

exercises.prompt_pt: Ele pede que eu ___ a verdade.
exercises.hint_en: He asks me to tell the truth. Verb: dizer.
exercises.explanation: From digo: drop -o, add -a. The subject changes from ele to eu, so the subjunctive is required.

exercises.hint_en: I hope to pass the exam. Verb: passar.
exercises.explanation: Same subject: the infinitive, not que + subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what does Lúcia want Pedro to take to Salvador?
exercises.explanation: Quero que você leve um casaco.

exercises.hint_en: I want you to be careful.

exercises.prompt: Match each subjunctive form with its verb

answers: Quero que você venha.
Eu quero que você venha.
Quero que vocês venham.
Eu quero que vocês venham.
exercises.explanation: Different subject, so que + subjunctive: venho gives venha.

exercises.prompt_en: Maybe she will come with us.
I hope he likes the gift.
answers: Espero que ele goste do presente.
Eu espero que ele goste do presente.
Tomara que ele goste do presente.
exercises.explanation: Hope is a trigger: gosto gives goste, since -ar verbs take e.

answers: Talvez ela chegue tarde.
Talvez ela chegue atrasada.
exercises.explanation: Talvez before the verb takes the subjunctive; chegar becomes chegue.

exercises.audio_pt: Que Deus te abençoe, meu filho.
exercises.hint_en: May God bless you, my son.

exercises.prompt_en: I ask you to be careful.
answers: Peço que você tome cuidado.
Eu peço que você tome cuidado.
Peço que você tenha cuidado.
Eu peço que você tenha cuidado.
Peço que vocês tomem cuidado.
Eu peço que vocês tomem cuidado.
Peço que vocês tenham cuidado.
Eu peço que vocês tenham cuidado.
exercises.explanation: Pedir que with a different subject takes the subjunctive: tomar gives tome and ter gives tenha.

exercises.prompt: Why does the verb stay in the indicative in 'Vejo que você está cansado'?
choices: Você can only take the indicative
Vejo reports a fact that the speaker observes
exercises.explanation: The subjunctive is triggered by the main clause's meaning. Verbs of seeing, knowing and saying report facts and take the indicative.

exercises.hint_en: I see that you are tired. Verb: estar.
exercises.explanation: Vejo que reports a fact, so the indicative está follows. Compare Lamento que você esteja cansado.

exercises.prompt: Why is the subjunctive of ficar written fique and not fice?
choices: Before e, c would be said s, so qu is written to keep the k sound
Every subjunctive form adds a u
A stress rule requires the u
exercises.explanation: The sound of c depends on the next letter: hard before a, o, u and soft before e, i. The ending changes to e, so qu is used to keep the k sound.

exercises.hint_en: I ask you to pay the bill. Verb: pagar.
exercises.explanation: Pago gives pague. Without the u, ge would be read zhe; gu keeps the hard g before e.

exercises.prompt_pt: Espero que ela ___ a trabalhar amanhã.
exercises.hint_en: I hope she starts working tomorrow. Verb: começar.
exercises.explanation: Começo gives comece. The cedilla is never written before e, because the plain c already says s there.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the subjunctive of conhecer for você?
exercises.explanation: The eu form conheço already has ç to keep the s sound before o; the ending a needs it again. Without the cedilla the c would say k.

exercises.hint_en: I want you (all) to sleep early today. Verb: dormir.
exercises.explanation: Durmo (the eu form) supplies the stem durm-, and the vocês ending for -ir verbs is -am.

exercises.hint_en: I hope you (all) are well. Verb: estar.
exercises.explanation: Estar is irregular: esteja, and the vocês form adds -m. The subject vocês needs the plural ending.

exercises.prompt: Why does vá carry a written accent?
choices: It marks the fusion of two words (crase)
It is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a vowel
It separates it from the word va
exercises.explanation: Stressed one-syllable words that end in a, e or o always take an accent: vá, dê, já, pé.

exercises.prompt: Why is deem (from dar, for vocês) written without an accent?
choices: Because deem is not a subjunctive form
Because dar is a regular verb
The stress is where the ending em predicts, so the old circumflex of dêem was dropped in 2009
exercises.explanation: Two strong vowels side by side are two syllables, DE-em. The default places the stress on the first e, so no mark is needed.

exercises.prompt: What does the leading que do in 'Que Deus te abençoe'?
choices: It turns the clause into a wish, like English 'may'
exercises.explanation: A blessing is a que clause standing alone with the main verb left out. The que stays and the subjunctive marks the wish.

exercises.prompt: In 'Que bom que você veio!', what is the first que?
exercises.explanation: The first que is the exclamation, as in Que pena! or Que delícia!, followed by an adjective and no verb. The second que is the conjunction.

exercises.prompt: How is the l in talvez pronounced?
exercises.explanation: An l that closes a syllable is said w, as in Brasil and Natal.

exercises.prompt: Why does ninguém carry a written accent?
choices: The accent shows a closed e
It is stressed on the last syllable, against the default for the ending em
It separates it from another word
exercises.explanation: Words ending in em default to stress on the second to last syllable. Ninguém breaks that default, so it needs a mark. The nasal sound comes from the m, and the u is silent after g.

exercises.prompt: How is the t in noite pronounced in most of Brazil?
choices: like ch in cheese, because the final e sounds like i
exercises.explanation: A t before the sound i, which includes a final e said i, becomes tch: NOI-tchi.

exercises.prompt: Why does cardápio have a written accent?
choices: The á is a nasal vowel
Stress on the third to last syllable always needs an accent
exercises.explanation: In car-DÁ-pi-o the ending io counts as two syllables, so the stress is third from last, and no ending predicts that.

exercises.prompt: Why is the subjunctive used in 'Fico feliz que você goste da casa', although the speaker knows you like it?
choices: Emotion triggers take the subjunctive: the speaker reacts to the fact instead of reporting it
exercises.explanation: Fico feliz que expresses a reaction. The mood marks that the content is not being reported.

exercises.hint_en: I hope you know the answer. Verb: saber.
exercises.explanation: Saber is one of the seven irregular verbs: eu sei does not give a stem, and the subjunctive is saiba.

exercises.prompt_en: I want us to go to the beach on Saturday.
answers: Quero que a gente vá à praia no sábado.
Eu quero que a gente vá à praia no sábado.
Quero que nós vamos à praia no sábado.
Quero que a gente vá pra praia no sábado.
Quero que nós vamos pra praia no sábado.
exercises.explanation: A gente takes the singular vá; the nós form is vamos. The à is the fusion of a (to) and a (the).

exercises.prompt_en: I ask you not to tell anyone.

choices: I ask you not to take long.
I ask you not to leave.
I ask you not to call.
I ask you not to forget.

exercises.audio_pt: Tomara que o ônibus não atrase.
exercises.hint_en: I hope the bus isn't late.
